name: Wilbur
facts: He was addressed by his dying grandfather as 'Willy'.
His grandfather told him to open the gates to Yog-Sothoth using a chant on page 751 of the complete edition.
His grandfather told him fire from earth cannot burn 'it'.
He was a scholar of tremendous erudition in his one-sided way.
He was known by correspondence to many librarians in distant places where rare and forbidden books are kept.
He was more and more hated and dreaded around Dunwich because of certain youthful disappearances suspected to be his doing.
He was able to silence inquiry through fear or through use of old-time gold that went forth for cattle-buying, as in his grandfather's time.
His height reached the normal adult limit and seemed inclined to wax beyond that figure.
In 1925 he was fully six and three-quarters feet tall when a scholarly correspondent from Miskatonic University called upon him.
He treated his half-deformed albino mother with growing contempt.
He forbade his mother to go to the hills with him on May Eve and Hallowmass.
In the summer of 1927 he repaired two sheds in the farmyard and began moving his books and effects out to them.
He was closing all doors and windows on the ground floor of the farmhouse and taking out partitions, as he and his grandfather had done upstairs four years before.
He was living in one of the sheds and seemed unusually worried and tremulous.
People suspected him of knowing something about his mother's disappearance.
His height had increased to more than seven feet and showed no signs of ceasing its development.
In the following winter he made his first trip outside the Dunwich region.
Correspondence with several great libraries failed to get him the loan of a book he desperately wanted, so he set out in person to consult the copy at Miskatonic.
He was almost eight feet tall and carried a cheap new valise from Osborn's general store when he appeared in Arkham.
He was described as a dark and goatish gargoyle.
He sought the Necronomicon of the mad Arab Alhazred in Olaus Wormius' Latin version, printed in Spain in the Seventeenth Century.
He had never seen a city before.
He passed heedlessly by a great white-fanged watchdog that barked at him with unnatural fury.

He began to collate the two texts to find a passage that would come on the 751st page of his own defective volume.
He told the librarian Henry Armitage he was looking for a formula or incantation containing the name Yog-Sothoth.
He found discrepancies, duplications, and ambiguities in the text that made determination difficult.
His grandfather muttered 'They didn't git him' after the death scene.

sources.quote: "More space, Willy, more space soon. Yew grows—an' that grows faster. It'll be ready to sarve ye soon, boy. Open up the gates to Yog-Sothoth with the long chant that ye'll find on page 751 of the complete edition, an' then put a match to the prison. Fire from airth can't burn it nohaow!"
"They didn't git him," he muttered in his heavy bass voice.

Wilbur was by this time a scholar of really tremendous erudition in his one-sided way, and was quietly known by correspondence to many librarians in distant places where rare and forbidden books of old days are kept.
In 1925, when a scholarly correspondent from Miskatonic University called upon him one day and departed pale and puzzled, he was fully six and three-quarters feet tall.
Through all the years Wilbur had treated his half-deformed albino mother with a growing contempt, finally forbidding her to go to the hills with him on May Eve and Hallowmass
In the summer of 1927 Wilbur repaired two sheds in the farmyard and began moving his books and effects out to them.
His height had increased to more than seven feet, and showed no signs of ceasing its development.

Almost eight feet tall, and carrying a cheap new valise from Osborn's general store, this dark and goatish gargoyle appeared one day in Arkham in quest of the dreaded volume kept under lock and key at the college library—the hideous Necronomicon of the mad Arab Alhazred in Olaus Wormius' Latin version, as printed in Spain in the Seventeenth Century.

He had never seen a city before, but had no thought save to find his way to the university grounds; where, indeed, he passed heedlessly by the great white-fanged watchdog that barked with unnatural fury and enmity, and tugged frantically at its stout chain.

Wilbur had with him the priceless but imperfect copy of Dr. Dee's English version which his grandfather had bequeathed him, and upon receiving access to the Latin copy he at once began to collate the two texts with the aim of discovering a certain passage which would have come on the 751st page of his own defective volume.

He was looking, he had to admit, for a kind of formula or incantation containing the frightful name Yog-Sothoth, and it puzzled him to find discrepancies, duplications, and ambiguities which made the matter of determination far from easy.

name: Lavinia
facts: She screamed at the way the whippoorwills followed the change during her father's death.
She sobbed at her father's death.
She was Wilbur's mother, half-deformed and albino.
In 1926 she complained to Mamie Bishop of being afraid of Wilbur.
She said there was more about him than she could tell, and more than she herself knew.
That Hallowe'en she was never seen again.
People generally suspected Wilbur of knowing something about his mother's disappearance.
fate: She disappeared after that Hallowe'en and was never seen again.

sources.quote: But speech gave place to gasps again, and Lavinia screamed at the way the whippoorwills followed the change.

Through all the years Wilbur had treated his half-deformed albino mother with a growing contempt, finally forbidding her to go to the hills with him on May Eve and Hallowmass; and in 1926 the poor creature complained to Mamie Bishop of being afraid of him.

"They's more abaout him as I knows than I kin tell ye, Mamie," she said, "an' naowadays they's more nor what I know myself. I vaow afur Gawd, I dun't know what he wants nor what he's a-tryin' to dew."
None of the countryfolk seemed to have died—but poor Lavinia Whateley, the twisted albino, was never seen again.

name: Henry Armitage
facts: He was the erudite librarian, A. M. Miskatonic, Ph. D. Princeton, Litt. D. Johns Hopkins.

He politely plied Wilbur with questions.
He looked involuntarily over Wilbur's shoulder at the open pages of the Latin Necronomicon as Wilbur copied a formula.
The left-hand page he looked at contained monstrous threats to the peace and sanity of the world.

sources.quote: This much he could not civilly refrain from telling the librarian—the same erudite Henry Armitage (A. M. Miskatonic, Ph. D. Princeton, Litt. D. Johns Hopkins) who had once called at the farm, and who now politely plied him with questions.

As he copied the formula he finally chose, Dr. Armitage looked involuntarily over his shoulder at the open pages; the left-hand one of which, in the Latin version, contained such monstrous threats to the peace and sanity of the world.
